about.automations.text:
What your hub does on its own: every automation and script in plain words, checked by fixed rules, with the entities it uses and when it last ran.

The views under the title show who switches what (with conflicts), the last 24 hours, the day plan, devices per room and the hub's health. Open an automation to see its flow and its findings; Show dependencies draws what sets an entity and what uses it.

Everything is read only: Lanloom never runs, changes or repairs anything in the hub. The flows need admin mode on the connection.
about.automations.title: Automations
about.devices.text:
Every device Lanloom found, with its type, how sure Lanloom is, maker, model and the services it offers. Search by name, address, maker or service.

Open a device to rename it, correct its type, hide it from the map or join two interfaces of the same device.

The Devices | Inventory switch opens the inventory: purpose, room, warranty, firmware and the end of its updates for every device, and what became of it.

The List | Stability switch shows how steady each device and connection was: 35 daily bars, availability over 24 hours and 7 days, the gaps of the last week, the typical repair time, and the wobbly ones to look at first.
about.devices.title: Devices
about.firewall.text: Your rules as zones and arrows, read from the router or controller. Changes are drafted here, checked in a dry run and applied only after you approve them – with a way back.
about.firewall.title: Firewall
about.map.text:
Your network drawn like a circuit board: every device is a component, every connection a trace. Moving dots are measured bytes – nothing is animated that was not measured.

The chips above the board filter by area or show only what is down. Click a component to open its card; the address follows, so the card can be shared and the back key closes it.
about.map.tips:
The colour of a dot at a component is its live grade (see the pill at the top right).
The board zooms with the mouse wheel or two fingers.
about.map.title: Map
about.network.text:
The same devices, ordered by how they are physically connected: which switch port or access point each one hangs on. Lanloom takes this from the controller, LLDP, address tables or what you entered by hand – the card of a device says which source decided.

Use the area chips to look at one network or one cabinet at a time.
about.network.title: Network
about.overview.text:
How your network is doing, in three seconds. The banner sums it up; the strip below it shows the last 24 hours in five-minute steps.

Every figure is a link: devices, what is online, what is new since yesterday, how fresh the sources are, the internet line and where your data went. The cards below list what stands out, the nightly report, new and uncertain devices and the last sign of life of every source.
about.overview.tips:
Click a figure to go to the details.
The page updates itself every few seconds; what you opened stays open.
about.overview.title: Overview
about.paths.text:
Where your data went: countries and devices over 24 hours, 7 or 30 days, from the flows Lanloom measured itself or received from your router. Lanloom never contacts the destinations.

Select a device to see only its paths; the full screen shows the world map large.
about.paths.title: Data paths
about.reports.text:
Every morning a short report of the night: outages, new devices, sources that failed, certificates that expire. Points that need a look can be ticked off.

Each report has its own address; the back key returns to the one you read before.
about.reports.title: Nightly report
about.running.text:
What runs on the other hosts of your network: containers, listening services, timers, failed services, and how loaded each host is. It needs the optional host agent on a host, or a container source for containers only.

Hosts with problems come first. Containers are also on the map, folded into their host; dashed lines show who talks to whom.

Everything is read only: Lanloom never starts, stops or changes anything on a host. Pair a host under Settings > Agents.
about.running.title: Running
about.settings.text: Scanning, connections to your router, controller and hub, appearance, users and security. Connections are read-only unless you switch on writing for a device family yourself.
about.settings.title: Settings
about.sites.text:
Every site you may see, at a glance: whether all is calm, how many devices are online, the internet and what stands out.

Each site has its own devices, connections, history and nightly report. Switch with the button next to the logo; your browser remembers the last site.
about.sites.tips:
The firewall editor and the AI assistant work on the home site.
Administrators release sites per person under Settings > Users.
A remote site is seen through its controller or a host agent - never by a scan across routers.
about.sites.title: All sites

settings.routes.text: Shows which networks and places the data passes on the way to the most important destinations of the data paths, with the time each section adds. Lanloom sends a few probe packets, rarely, towards your most important destinations; number and interval are adjustable.

settings.routes.consent: Switched on, Lanloom measures the routes from this host: one small probe packet per hop (at most 32 per destination and measurement) towards the destination groups with the most traffic, each at most once per interval, never while the machine is busy, in a worker thread with the lowest priority. It also asks the system's name resolver for the names of the answering routers. The address of a destination is used only for its measurement and never stored. Stored for 30 days are only the networks, operators, cities and time bands of each route, never an address or a host name. It works with ordinary sockets: the standard container needs no extra rights for this.

Switched on, Lanloom fetches three public lists of exchange points from www.peeringdb.com (at most one check a day, a new copy a month) and keeps them only for this instance's own diagnosis; they are never passed on, exported or bundled, and switching off deletes them. Without it, exchange points are recognised from router names.

setup.guide.controller.1: Open the controller's web page and sign in as an administrator.
setup.guide.controller.2: Add a new local user (not a cloud account) for Lanloom.

setup.guide.dns.1: Open the filter's web page and sign in as an administrator.
setup.guide.dns.2: Create an access just for Lanloom: an application password or a user of its own.
setup.guide.dns.3: Lanloom only reads totals (queries and blocked share per hour, the top lists, the resolvers and the block lists) and never asks for single queries.

setup.guide.dns.title: Create a separate read access
setup.guide.apikey.1: Open the firewall's web interface and sign in as an administrator.
setup.guide.apikey.2: Create a user just for Lanloom (no shell, no other access) and give it only the pages Lanloom reads: firewall rules, aliases, interface overview and groups, NAT, address reservations, routes, gateways and VPN status. The adapter guide lists them.
setup.guide.apikey.3: Create an API key for that user and keep the downloaded file safe. The firewall's privileges do not separate reading from writing; Lanloom itself only ever sends read requests.
setup.guide.apikey.4: Enter the address, the key and the secret below, then press Test.
setup.guide.apikey.title: Create an API key of its own
setup.guide.ubus.1: Sign in to the router over SSH as an administrator.
setup.guide.ubus.2: Add an access list that only allows reading (the file from the adapter guide) and a login just for Lanloom that uses only this list. The router's own administrator account is not needed.
setup.guide.ubus.3: Restart the router's access service so the new login works. Lanloom refuses a login whose list allows any change.
setup.guide.ubus.4: Enter the address, the login name and the password below, then press Test.
setup.guide.ubus.title: Create a read-only login
setup.guide.family.1: Open the device's web page and sign in as an administrator.
setup.guide.family.2: Create an API key or a local user just for Lanloom (no cloud account).
setup.guide.family.3: Give it read-only rights only; Lanloom refuses keys that can change anything.
setup.guide.family.4: Enter the address and the key or the user below, then press Test. The adapter guide in the documentation has the details for your model.
setup.guide.family.title: Create a read-only key
setup.guide.tr064.1: Open the box's web page and sign in. Under Home Network › Network › Network Settings allow access for applications (TR-064).
setup.guide.tr064.2: Under System › Users add a user just for Lanloom with a long password of its own, with access from the home network only.
setup.guide.tr064.3: Give it the right to the box settings (TR-064 needs it); Lanloom only sends queries that read and cannot change anything. Never use your own account.
setup.guide.tr064.4: Enter the address and the user below, then press Test. Leave the port out: Lanloom uses 49000 (or 49443 for https).
setup.guide.tr064.title: Create a user for Lanloom
setup.guide.hub.1: Open the hub's web page and sign in.
setup.guide.hub.2: Optionally create a separate user for Lanloom that is not an administrator.
setup.guide.hub.3: In that user's profile, create a long-lived access token and copy it right away (it is shown only once).
setup.guide.hub.4: Enter the hub address and paste the token below, then press Test.
setup.guide.hub.title: Create an access token
setup.guide.hv.1: Open the hypervisor's web page and sign in as an administrator.
setup.guide.hv.2: Create an API token for a user, with privilege separation switched on.
setup.guide.hv.3: Give the token only the built-in auditor (read-only) role on the root path; Lanloom refuses tokens that can change anything.
setup.guide.hv.4: Enter the address, the token ID and the secret below, then press Test.
setup.guide.hv.title: Create a read-only API token
setup.guide.mqtt.1: Open the broker's configuration or its user management.
setup.guide.mqtt.2: Add a user for Lanloom with a password of its own.
setup.guide.mqtt.3: Allow it to read (subscribe to) the topics only, not to publish.
setup.guide.mqtt.4: Enter host, port, user name and password below (TLS if the broker uses it), then press Test.
setup.guide.mqtt.title: Create a read-only user

setup.guide.snmp.2: Switch SNMP on; prefer version 3 with a user, authentication and encryption.
setup.guide.snmp.3: Grant read-only access, ideally only for the address of this host.
setup.guide.snmp.4: Enter the device address and the community or the version 3 user below, then press Test.

about.incidents.title: Incidents
about.incidents.text:
Faults bundled into incidents: what went down together, which part probably took the others with it, how long it lasted and what changed before.

The calendar shows the last 90 days, the heatmap the hours of the last week. Events list everything the journal noted; Timeline & data state keeps firmware jumps, own updates, new devices and long outages for more than a year.
about.incidents.tips:
Play in rewind shows the moment on the map; R opens the rewind on any map, Space plays, Esc goes back to live.
Sure means the parts hang on the root in the failure chain; probably means the root was not seen down itself.
Lanloom's own updates and the time inside a maintenance window count as maintenance, never as a fault.

about.controlroom.title: Control room
about.controlroom.text:
What keeps the network and the house running, on one page: the internet with what the gateway says and what is measured, the storage boxes, the battery backup and the backups.

Every block says how old its picture is. A reading that went quiet is dimmed and counts as unknown, never as fine. What needs a look is listed on top.

Press a block to jump to its part of the page.
The outside check of the internet only runs after an administrator picked the targets.
A backup nobody restored is only a hope: note the day you tried it.
